_version.redaction_note: All stimuli are generated from the physics core and the noise model. No real object identifiers appear in any prompt or answer.

_design_note: Every item uses a production response format. There is no multiple-choice format anywhere in this bank and the schema does not permit one. If the answer is visible on screen the operator is pattern-matching rather than retrieving, and the retention benefit is largely lost. Distractors live in the reject list and are used only after the operator has committed, to teach in the explanation.

drills.prompt: What has happened to this object, and what is your first action?

accept: manoeuvre
possible manoeuvre
in-plane manoeuvre
period change

partial.note: Correct but imprecise. Name the departure type: this is in-plane, which points to in-track or radial.

reject.why_wrong: The observations depart from the zero line and stay departed across multiple points. That is not noise.
A residual departure says the object is not where its state predicts. It says nothing about headcount.

drills.explain: Observations on the zero line mean the current observations agree with the current state. A sustained departure means they no longer do. Because the departure is in-plane, the burn was in-track or radial rather than cross-track. First action is always to verify epoch age and observation density before believing it, because a starved or stale fit produces the same picture.

drills.prompt: The provider has labelled this a possible manoeuvre. Do you agree, and why?

accept: no, the observation gap means the fit decayed
not assessable, request observations covering the gap
cannot confirm, propagation error is as likely

partial.note: Right call, but the reason is the marking. Name the gap and the starved fit.

reject.why_wrong: The departure follows a long observation gap with a starved fit either side. Accumulated propagation error produces exactly this picture and is the more parsimonious explanation until ruled out.

drills.explain: A manoeuvre departs from a well-constrained fit. Propagation error departs from a starved one. The discriminator is observation density either side of the departure, not the size of the departure. This is why the product standard requires observations preceding and during any suspected manoeuvre. Challenging a provider assessment is a competency, not an impertinence.

drills.prompt: From the Delta column alone, name the burn direction.

accept: in-track
in track boost
along-track

reject.why_wrong: A radial burn leaves the period alone. The period has changed here.
Cross-track changes inclination or RAAN. Both are essentially unchanged here.

drills.explain: The element signature identifies the burn without anyone telling you. In-track changes period, eccentricity and possibly argument of perigee. Radial changes eccentricity and argument of perigee but leaves period alone. Cross-track changes inclination or RAAN. Period is the fastest discriminator: if it moved, the burn had an in-track component.

drills.prompt: Given this altitude change, estimate the resulting longitude drift rate in degrees per day, and state the direction.

accept: computed_from_params

reject.why_wrong: A boost raises average altitude, which raises the period, which means the object falls behind. Higher is slower.

drills.explain: Higher is slower. A boost raises average altitude and the object drifts backward; a de-boost lowers it and the object drifts forward. Carrying the approximate relationship between altitude difference and drift rate lets you sanity-check a reported figure in seconds, which is how you catch an artefact before it becomes a report.

drills.prompt: The tooling reports this drift rate. What do you do?

accept: reject the value, check epoch separation
artefact, the epochs are too close together
impossible, division by a near-zero time gap

partial.note: Right instinct. Now name the mechanism: near-zero epoch separation in the denominator.

reject.why_wrong: No object can drift at this rate. A physically impossible number is an arithmetic artefact until proven otherwise, and reporting it costs credibility that is hard to recover.

drills.explain: Two element sets separated by a near-zero epoch gap produce a longitude difference divided by almost nothing, and the quotient diverges. The object has not moved unusually at all. Check the epoch separation of the inputs before believing any derived rate. Carrying a rough sense of what is physically possible is the filter that catches this in a glance.

drills.prompt: Classify this relative motion and state whether the object is spending fuel to maintain it.

accept: natural motion circumnavigation
NMC
natural motion, no fuel

partial.note: Correct family. The distinction between natural and forced is the operationally important part, because it tells you whether fuel is being spent.

reject.why_wrong: Forced motion changes shape at discrete points. This geometry repeats identically across every revolution, which is the signature of unforced natural motion.

drills.explain: A closed ellipse around the origin, traced once per orbit, with in-track extent roughly twice the radial extent, repeating unchanged, is a natural motion circumnavigation. It costs nothing to maintain, which means the object can sit there indefinitely. That is a different warning from forced motion, which burns fuel continuously and therefore signals sustained deliberate attention.

drills.prompt: Classify this geometry and state what you would check next.

accept: drifting NMC, check whether the drift is slowing
drifting natural motion circumnavigation
series of close approaches

partial.note: Plot enough revolutions and the walk along the in-track axis becomes visible. A short window makes a drifting NMC look stable.

reject.why_wrong: A perch holds a standoff distance. This geometry is still moving past, revolution by revolution.

drills.explain: The ellipse repeats but walks along the in-track axis. The object is in proximity for several revolutions without being stationed there. The critical follow-up is whether the drift rate is decreasing, because a slowing drift near an asset of interest indicates an intent to stabilise, and that is a materially more serious assessment than a transit.

drills.prompt: How many manoeuvres are visible in this relative motion?

accept: computed_from_params

reject.why_wrong: Each discontinuity in the relative motion geometry is a burn. Natural motion repeats identically; this does not.

drills.explain: Forced motion circumnavigation shapes the relationship actively, and every change of geometry is a manoeuvre. Counting them gives you cumulative delta-v, and cumulative delta-v is the clearest available proxy for how much the operator of that object cares about this relationship.

drills.prompt: State your assessment and your immediate action.

accept: precision plane match, notify higher headquarters, maximise tasking
deliberate plane match, escalate and uprank

partial.note: Correct read. The action is the scored part: this requires prompt notification, not observation.

reject.why_wrong: A precision plane match requires specific knowledge of the target orbit, costs significant fuel, and places the object in immediate proximity capability. It is a recognised indicator of a prelude to further activity and warrants an immediate response.

drills.explain: Plane matching is fuel intensive, so precision matching is never accidental. The deltas have also been held for days, which costs more fuel still. Recognition alone is not the competency; the competency is that recognition triggers notification and tasking without further deliberation.

drills.prompt: The current RAAN delta is large. Is this object a concern?

accept: yes, raDot is closing the planes and days to closure is finite
yes, slow plane match in progress via altitude

partial.note: Right, but name the mechanism. The current delta is irrelevant; the closure rate is the finding.

reject.value: no, the planes are far apart
reject.why_wrong: The current delta is a snapshot. raDot tells you it is closing, and days to closure is effectively a countdown. This is the patient, fuel-cheap route to a plane match and it is easy to miss because nothing dramatic happens on any given day.

drills.explain: Altitude affects the rate at which RAAN precesses. An adversary can accept a long timeline in exchange for a fraction of the fuel cost of a direct plane change. The days-to-closure column is the one that matters, which is exactly why the product standard requires raDot and days to RAAN closure on every COCO table.

drills.prompt: This close approach distance looks alarming. What do you do first?

accept: check the epoch age before anything else
request an updated state, do not escalate yet

reject.why_wrong: The distance was propagated from a state days old. The uncertainty far exceeds the reported miss distance, so the number is precise and meaningless. Escalating on it spends credibility you will need later.

drills.explain: Read the epoch column before the distance column, every single time. This is the first analytical step in predictive surveillance for a reason. A distance computed from a stale state is a hypothesis, not a measurement.

drills.prompt: A step change is visible. What do you request before assessing it?

accept: hemisphere view
sensor view
the phase angles at which the change was observed
extended view

partial.note: Right direction. Name which supporting view and why: hemisphere for bias, sensor for a single-sensor artefact, phase angles for geometry.

reject.why_wrong: Three benign explanations are outstanding: phase angle geometry, a single-sensor artefact, and hemispheric bias. Each has a specific product that eliminates it. Reporting before eliminating them is how a sensor story becomes a satellite story.

drills.explain: The product standard requires a supporting view alongside the seven-day overlay precisely because a step change has three common benign causes. The hemisphere view removes hemispheric bias, the sensor view removes a single-sensor artefact, and stating the phase angles removes geometry. Rank these as peer hypotheses, not footnotes.

drills.prompt: Headcount of two on a red parent. Which procedure, and what is step one?

accept: separation, confirm the headcount across more than one pass
separation processing, verify the count first

partial.note: Correct procedure. Step one is confirming the count, because a false headcount sends the entire response down the wrong path.

reject.why_wrong: Breakup starts at three or more, and the discriminator is intent. A co-timed parent manoeuvre points to a deliberate release.
UCT discovery applies to a headcount of two on a blue parent. This parent is red.

drills.explain: The branch is: three or more starts as breakup; two on a red parent is separation; two on a blue parent is UCT discovery. Count sets the default but intent can override it in either direction. Confirm the count across passes before committing, because a tracking artefact that produces a false headcount costs the whole response.

drills.prompt: Headcount of two on a blue parent. Which procedure, and is a report required?

accept: UCT discovery, reporting is decided with higher headquarters not automatic
UCT discovery, a report is not automatic

partial.note: Correct procedure. The reporting nuance is the scored part and it is the one operators most often get wrong.

reject.why_wrong: For UCT discovery a report is not always sent. Whether one is published is a decision taken with higher headquarters at the time of discovery.
Separation applies to a red parent.

drills.explain: This is the discrimination operators most often miss, because the three branches look similar and only one of them has a conditional reporting obligation. Publishing by default is as much an error as failing to report. The decision and its rationale must be recorded either way.

drills.prompt: Optical shows one object where there were two. Have they docked?

accept: no, RF still separates them, assess as unresolved
cannot conclude, cross-tagging expected at this separation
unresolved rather than docked

partial.note: Right, and the reason is the marking. Name RF separability as the discriminator.

reject.why_wrong: Electro-optical sensors fuse objects at these separations, so a merged optical picture is expected and is not evidence of contact. A second phenomenology still separates them, which means they are unresolved, not merged.

drills.explain: Cross-tagging has been observed from around ten kilometres, with optical fusion between roughly two and five kilometres, while radio frequency signatures remained distinguishable throughout, particularly where the objects used different bands. A docking assessment needs sustained single-object detection across phenomenologies. Consider merged-conditions terminology rather than asserting docking, which avoids speculating beyond the evidence.

drills.prompt: What has happened, and what is your first action?

accept: breakup, secure optical collection and confirm headcount
fragmentation, uprank tasking for optical passes

partial.note: Correct read. The action is what buys you the evidence: secure the optical pass using the pass schedule.

reject.why_wrong: A glint is a brief specular spike that returns to baseline. This does not return, and the spread of observations widens, which means many new reflecting surfaces.
An attitude change alters the shape of the curve. It does not widen the spread of magnitudes this way.

drills.explain: A large sudden brightening with a widening spread is the photometric signature of a fragmentation, because many new surfaces are now reflecting. It also brackets the event time. The immediate action is to secure optical collection, since optical is what establishes headcount in the belt and headcount is what confirms the event.

drills.prompt: Observations have stopped entirely on an object of interest. What is your assessment?

accept: check solar exclusion and eclipse before concluding anything
not assessable, the object is in exclusion
absence during predicted exclusion is not evidence

partial.note: Right. Name the geometry and state it as a limitation in the report rather than as a finding.

reject.why_wrong: An absence of data during a predicted exclusion is not evidence of anything. At higher altitudes an object can sit in exclusion for days.
You cannot infer motion from an absence you already expected.

drills.explain: Establish the collection geometry before drawing any conclusion from silence. The Intelsat 33E event occurred during solar exclusion with passive RF signals also dropping away, and the collection plan had to be worked around it. State the gap as a limitation in any report; a gap you have named is a finding, a gap you have missed is an error.

drills.prompt: The neighbourhood looks clear. Do you report nothing?

accept: no, ask what filter was applied and request the unfiltered view
no, this is HRR filtered and may hide unranked objects

reject.why_wrong: An absence in a filtered product is not an absence in reality. This view is ranked-objects-only, and objects acquire relevance before they acquire a rank.

drills.explain: Always ask what filter produced the product in front of you. A ranked-only neighbourhood has previously hidden the objects that actually mattered, which is why the standard now asks for both an HRR-plus-UCT view and an HRR-only view, and why a distance filter should not be applied at all.

drills.prompt: Nothing has happened for several weeks. Is there anything to report?

accept: yes, the station-keeping pattern has stopped and the object is now drifting
yes, the cessation is the finding

partial.note: Correct observation. The reportable insight is that an established pattern broke, which speaks to a change of state in the object.

reject.why_wrong: The absence of the expected burn is the signal. An object that stops station-keeping has changed state: fuel, fault, mission change, or deliberate repositioning.

drills.explain: Intent is read against a baseline. An object that starts doing something new is obvious; an object that stops doing something routine is not, and it is often the more informative of the two. Compare against several cycles of the object's own history, and confirm observations exist across the period so you are not reading a collection gap as a cessation.

drills.prompt: Against which longitude do you run the target assessment?

accept: the ascending-side belt penetration point
where it crosses the belt on the way up

reject.why_wrong: Apogee is above the belt in this case, so the trajectory passes through the belt on the way up and again on the way down. The threat is at the ascending crossing, not at apogee.

drills.explain: Two cases, two different longitudes. If apogee is at or below belt altitude, assess against the longitude at or directly above apogee. If apogee is above it, assess against the ascending-side penetration point. Choosing the wrong one invalidates the entire target list and therefore the entire warning, which is why this is step one of the procedure.

drills.prompt: Describe what this object has done.

accept: drifted then stopped drift and parked
drift stop
stopped at a longitude

partial.note: Read to the bottom. The trace flattens to vertical, which is a drift stop.

reject.why_wrong: The trace flattens, meaning longitude stops changing with time. That is stopping, not accelerating.

drills.explain: Time runs down the page with newest at the bottom. Sloped means drifting, steeper means faster, vertical means parked. Confirm the orientation before reading any waterfall, because a provider putting newest at the top inverts every drift direction you read off it.

drills.prompt: Two traces are converging. What do you request before assessing this?

accept: neighbourhood constrained by inclination and RAAN
the plane relationship
inclination and RAAN deltas

reject.value: nothing, this is a close approach
reject.why_wrong: The waterfall shows longitude only. Two objects can share a longitude while being widely separated in plane, in which case they pass quickly and neither can linger.

drills.explain: Longitude convergence alone is not proximity. The waterfall is a one-dimensional view of a three-dimensional relationship and it cannot tell you whether these objects will come anywhere near each other. Knowing what a product cannot tell you is as much a competency as knowing what it can.

drills.prompt: You cannot find a state for this object. Is it untracked?

accept: no, search for observations and ask providers directly
no, it may be tracked as a UCT with observations but no published state

reject.why_wrong: Absence of a state is not absence of data. A provider may be tracking the object as an uncorrelated track, publishing observations without publishing a state.

drills.explain: Search for observations, not only states, and ask providers directly what they hold. This exact situation has previously delayed characterisation of a newly separated object: the tracking existed and the state did not, so nothing surfaced through the usual route.

drills.prompt: Name the burn direction and state why it matters.

accept: cross-track, it changes inclination or RAAN and is fuel expensive
cross-track, expensive therefore deliberate

partial.note: Correct direction. The significance is the scored part: cross-track is expensive, and expense signals intent.

reject.why_wrong: An in-track burn appears in the in-plane residual component. This departure is out of plane.

drills.explain: Out-of-plane residuals point to a cross-track burn, which changes inclination or RAAN. Plane changes are the most fuel-expensive routine manoeuvre available, so an object spending that fuel is making a statement about intent. Check immediately whether it is a plane match in progress against something you care about.

drills.prompt: The marker tooltip gives a period change and an inclination change. Name the burn direction.

accept: in-plane
in-track
in-track or radial

partial.note: Correct exclusion. Now name what it is: a period change with negligible inclination change is in-plane.

reject.why_wrong: The inclination change is negligible. Cross-track burns change inclination or RAAN, and this one has not.

drills.explain: The product hands you both deltas at the candidate time, so the burn family can be named in seconds without waiting for a DC table. A period change with essentially no inclination change is in-plane. A meaningful inclination change is cross-track and therefore the expensive, deliberate kind.

drills.prompt: There are six marks along this track. How many manoeuvres have occurred?

reject.why_wrong: Those are state change markers, indicating the orbit solution was refitted. A solution can be updated many times without the object moving. The geometry continues smoothly through every one of them.

drills.explain: State change markers and manoeuvres are different things and they look similar. A manoeuvre changes the geometry; a state update changes the solution. Check the residuals for the same period before attributing any mark to a burn, and note which object each mark belongs to, because the product distinguishes reference from non-reference.

drills.prompt: Which object on this neighbourhood most warrants attention, and why?

accept: the distant object with the low delta-v
the one that could close cheapest
low delta-v regardless of current distance

partial.note: Distance is the weaker signal. An object that would need an expensive burn to close is less of a proposition than a distant one that could close cheaply.

reject.why_wrong: Score is a provider heuristic blending factors you did not choose. Use it as an input, not as the answer.

drills.explain: The delta-v column gives the cost of opportunity directly. Cost is the proxy for how quickly a relationship could change, which makes it a better guide than current separation. Read it alongside plane deltas and epoch age, and treat the provider score as one more input rather than a conclusion.

drills.prompt: Before reading any row, what two things do you check in the header?

accept: the filter toggle state and the threshold block
only HRR toggle and the constraints applied

partial.note: Half of it. The filter toggles are the other half, and the ranked-objects-only toggle is the one that hides things.

reject.why_wrong: Epoch is the first thing you read in the body, and it is right. But the header tells you what was excluded before you ever got a body to read.

drills.explain: The threshold block states the longitude, inclination and drift constraints applied. The filter toggles state whether ranked objects only, or uncorrelated tracks only, are being shown. Both are one click and neither announces itself. An absence in a filtered product is not an absence in reality.

drills.prompt: How do you tell whether this object has changed?

accept: compare intervals at matched phase angle
look for a later interval sitting off the earlier curve at the same phase angle

partial.note: Yes, and the matching matters: compare at the same phase angle, because that is what the axis choice exists to enable.

reject.value: look for a slope across the plot
reject.why_wrong: The horizontal axis is phase angle, not time. The rise and fall across the plot is the expected brightness function of viewing geometry.

drills.explain: Plotting magnitude against solar equatorial phase angle is how the geometry effect is controlled for. The object's own curve is the baseline, and change is a later interval departing from it at matched phase angle. Note also that asymmetry either side of zero is common and expected, so compare against this object's established shape rather than against symmetry.

drills.prompt: Find the drifting object and state its direction of drift.

accept: computed_from_params

partial.note: Found it. Direction comes from the gradient, and the gradient only reads correctly once you have confirmed newest is at the bottom.

reject.why_wrong: Dense clusters are populated longitude regions where objects live. They carry no meaning by themselves. Structure that moves across longitude with time is the signal.
The empty horizontal bands are collection gaps rather than empty sky, and the drifting streak is present outside them.

drills.explain: A real waterfall carries tens of thousands of observations. Picking a single drifting object out of that density is the trained skill, and the technique is to follow the colour rather than to look for a shape. Confirm the time direction before reading any gradient, because an inverted plot reverses every drift direction you read off it.

drills.prompt: Mean anomaly has changed substantially between consecutive states while other elements barely moved. What does this support?

accept: a separation or a significant in-track event
the object is not where the previous solution placed it in its orbit

partial.note: Possible, and the in-track angle difference between parent and new object is the specific evidence that supports separation.

reject.why_wrong: Inclination and RAAN have barely moved. Mean anomaly is position within the orbit, not orientation of it.

drills.explain: Mean anomaly is position within the orbit, so a jump relative to what propagation predicts means the object is not where the previous solution placed it. Comparing the parent's mean anomaly against a new object's expresses their in-track separation as an angle, which is a fast way to characterise the geometry. Rule out a cross-tag first, because a swapped identity produces the same apparent jump.

drills.prompt: Six hours on, you feel more confident but no new evidence has arrived. Do you publish a verified report?

accept: no, nothing new has arrived, keep the possible register
no, but publish again in the possible register if the picture has moved

reject.why_wrong: Familiarity is not evidence. The verified register changes what the recipient is expected to do, so it needs an observation behind it, not elapsed time.

drills.explain: The move from possible to verified is the primary confidence signal in the whole report and it must be earned by a specific observation. Name what changed. If nothing has, publishing again in the possible register is entirely correct and is expected on a developing event.

drills.prompt: An object crosses the primary's longitude in two days. Is that when they are closest?

accept: no, plane separation means longitude match is not closest approach
no, the minimum distance time is a separate column and may differ

reject.why_wrong: Longitude crossing and closest approach are different instants. Two objects can share a longitude while being widely separated in plane, which is why the product carries both columns.

drills.explain: Days to longitude crossing is a tasking countdown; absolute and next minimum distance with their times are the approach geometry. Reading one for the other produces tasking windows aimed at the wrong moment.

drills.prompt: Which association has departed, and what does that tell you?

accept: beta, so out-of-plane, a cross-track burn
beta association, inclination or RAAN change

partial.note: Correct read. The consequence is the scored part: out-of-plane means cross-track, which is expensive and therefore deliberate.

reject.why_wrong: Time association is stable here. It carries the in-plane story and would depart on a period or in-track change.

drills.explain: Time association carries in-plane, beta association carries out-of-plane. Identifying which one departed narrows the burn family before you look at a single number, and out-of-plane immediately raises the significance because plane changes are the most fuel-expensive routine manoeuvre available.

drills.prompt: Four minutes in. Products are still arriving and the target list is provisional. What do you do now?

accept: publish a one-sentence alert now, analysis follows
make the verbal call and release a holding report
release now and say further analysis will follow

partial.note: Half of it. The written alert goes out too, and it can be one sentence.

reject.why_wrong: A sentence saying the target list will follow is a complete and correct report. Waiting for it has repeatedly cost this cell twenty to thirty minutes of a recipient's planning time.

reject.value: wait for the products to complete
reject.why_wrong: The clock started when the indication arrived. The recipient needs planning time more than they need your certainty.

drills.explain: The published standard is two-legged: 60 minutes from initial indications, or 30 from the last provider product, whichever is earlier. Providers have not yet dropped, so the 60 minute leg governs for now and will tighten to 30 from their drop the moment they do. Exercise assessments recorded events at 55 and 61 minutes as late, judged against the tighter leg. A one-sentence alert buys the recipient planning time and everything else follows in later reports.

drills.prompt: A provider has just posted this. What is your next action?

accept: transition the thread to the proximity procedure now
start the RPO checklist immediately

partial.value: assess whether it is an RPO
partial.note: That assessment happens inside the procedure, not before entering it. Transition first.

reject.value: discuss with the site lead whether to transition
reject.why_wrong: This product is the trigger. Discussion before transition is exactly the delay recorded on at least five separate events across one exercise, in each case assessed as could have been initiated earlier.

reject.value: wait for confirmation from a second product
reject.why_wrong: Backing out of a procedure entered early costs minutes. Entering it late has repeatedly cost hours.

drills.explain: A relative motion product showing circumnavigation entry is a trigger, not a topic. This is the single most repeated procedural delay in the exercise record, and the recommended fix was an automatic transition on exactly this cue. Transition, then assess inside the procedure.

drills.prompt: Twelve open threads, more arriving. What do you do first?

accept: triage into active, monitoring and ready to close
sweep for untouched ripe threads and close the resolved ones
name what you are not working

partial.note: Right instinct, but the triage has to be explicit and stated, or the threads you are not working simply get dropped silently.

reject.why_wrong: Recency is not priority. The oldest untouched ripe thread is usually the costliest to leave, and one proximity event was recorded as un-actioned for at least an hour under exactly these conditions.
Peak concurrent load reached around thirty-five in one exercise. Resolved threads left open consume the attention that emerging events need.

drills.explain: Under overload something will be dropped, and the only question is whether you choose it. Explicit triage into active, monitoring and ready to close, a ceiling of around three concurrent critical threads per analyst, and an ageing callout at fifteen to twenty minutes are the recorded recommendations. Closing what is finished is not administrative tidiness, it is how you free attention for what is not.

drills.prompt: You notice an indication posted eighteen minutes ago that no one has picked up. When did your reporting clock start?

accept: eighteen minutes ago, when it was posted
when it was posted, not when I saw it

reject.why_wrong: The clock runs from the indication, not from the noticing. Eighteen minutes are already gone against whichever leg governs.

drills.explain: Latency is measured from when the indication appeared, which is the only fair way to score proactive monitoring. The exercise record notes that once cued this cell performs well and the lag is entirely in the noticing.

drills.prompt: This draft is ready for release. Anything to fix?

accept: an unfilled placeholder and a reference to something not included
template text left in and a dangling target list reference

partial.note: Found one. There is also a reference to something the report does not include, which needs either the content or a sentence saying it will follow.

reject.why_wrong: A published report retaining unfilled template text was recorded in the exercise register. One end-to-end read before release catches it.

drills.explain: Two failures recorded together in the exercise register: template placeholders surviving into a published report, and a report stating a target list had been developed without including it or saying when it would follow. Either the content goes in, or a sentence says it is coming. One read end to end before release is the whole fix.

drills.prompt: You are making a verbal call on the second of two concurrent separation events. What must the call contain?

accept: the identifier and role of each object, and the times, stated explicitly
which is parent and which is child, by identifier, with times

partial.note: Necessary but not sufficient. Which one is the parent and which the child is the part that was recorded as missing.

reject.value: a summary, the detail is in the thread
reject.why_wrong: A verbal report on a second concurrent event that lacked firm object identification and clarity of parent and child was recorded as introducing confusion during a time-sensitive window. The recipient has your sentence, not your thread.

drills.explain: The first report on one exercise day was assessed as well-structured and confident; the second, on a concurrent event and by a different operator, lacked firm object identification and clarity of parent and child. Same crew, same day. The difference was structure under load, which is what drilling it produces.

drills.prompt: Fragmentation evidence has arrived and there is no launch indication for it. What do you conclude?

accept: reason backwards from the effect and start breakup processing
work the fragmentation now and look for a cause in parallel

partial.note: Correct read. The action is the scored part: start the procedure that governs the effect rather than waiting for the trigger you expected.

reject.value: wait for the launch confirmation before acting
reject.why_wrong: Evidence does not arrive in the order the procedure describes. A debris cloud report arriving before launch confirmation was recorded as causing temporary confusion and slowing situational awareness, precisely because the crew waited for the expected sequence.

drills.explain: Reality does not supply a canonical sequence. When the consequence arrives first, reason backwards to the likely cause and start the procedure that governs what you can actually see. The missing indication is a question to pursue in parallel, not a precondition for acting.

drills.prompt: This sits just outside the reporting threshold. Do you report?

accept: raise the judgement rather than absorbing it, with a recommendation and a confidence level
report it, stating that it is below threshold and why it still matters given the trend
escalate the call to the site lead with a recommendation

partial.note: Defensible. The scored part is that you state the reasoning and the confidence rather than simply deciding.
Also defensible on the threshold alone. The scored part is that you raise the judgement rather than closing it silently.

reject.value: no, it is below threshold, nothing to do
reject.why_wrong: The deliberation is itself the signal. Sub-threshold proximity was explicitly recorded as an area where crews were uncertain and where discretion exists but needs support. Silently resolving it removes the chance for that support.

drills.explain: This one has no single right answer and the trainer does not pretend otherwise. Sub-threshold proximity is a recorded policy ambiguity. What is scored is the reasoning: the threshold, the trend, the significance of the asset, a stated recommendation with a confidence level, and raising it rather than absorbing it. The debrief shows expert reasoning in both directions.

drills.prompt: You have taken the handover. What do you do before starting work?

accept: check the open thread list against what was briefed and close the gap
identify the threads not covered in the brief and establish their state

partial.note: You have inherited two threads that were not briefed, and one of them is ripe. The gap is now yours.

reject.why_wrong: The previous shift may have been at the end of a long period; fatigue on handover is a recorded and expected condition rather than a failing. Checking the thread list against the brief is how you catch what fatigue dropped.

drills.explain: The foundation of a successful shift is a solid handover, and the exercise record shows both directions clearly: a comprehensive handover produced a strong opening posture, a rushed one produced a slow start and missed injects. You cannot control the quality of what you are given. You can always reconcile the brief against the open thread list.

drills.prompt: A radar observation is reported at this range. Do you use it?

accept: no, no contracted radar reaches that range, it is a data problem
no, reject it and check whether other data from that source is affected

partial.note: Right call. Name the reason: the range exceeds the performance envelope of the sensor type.

reject.why_wrong: An observation requiring a capability the network does not have is a data problem rather than a discovery. This was observed in exercise conditions and disrupted a provider pipeline.

drills.explain: Check an observation against the performance envelope of the sensor type that supposedly produced it. Contamination, mislabelling and pipeline faults all present as data that looks like capability. Having rejected it, check whether other data from the same source is affected before relying on any of it.

drills.prompt: Twenty-two minutes in, analysis progressing well. The required notification calls have not been made. What now?

accept: make the calls now, they do not wait on the assessment
make the notifications immediately, then continue the analysis

reject.value: finish the assessment first so there is something worth saying
reject.why_wrong: The notification and the assessment are separate obligations with separate timings. Skipping mandatory calls was recorded as a trend across multiple exercise periods, assessed as complacency or as critical steps not standing out in a dense checklist.

drills.explain: No amount of good analysis substitutes for a skipped mandatory step. This one recurs across exercise periods and is a discipline habit rather than a knowledge gap, which is exactly the kind of thing repetition fixes.

drills.prompt: You have inherited a single thread covering several objects in one combined proximity event. The procedure does not describe this. What do you do?

accept: decide how to proceed, state the decision and reasoning, continue
split or keep combined on the basis of what serves the recipient, and say which you chose

partial.note: A reasonable choice. The scored part is stating the decision and the reasoning so the next shift is not confused in turn.

reject.value: ask for guidance and hold until it arrives
reject.why_wrong: A combined thread handed over in this shape was recorded as causing processing uncertainty, and the assessment was that non-routine workflows are not rehearsed or that deviation is treated as impermissible. Under surge conditions, stalling is the failure. Deviating with stated judgement is not.

drills.explain: Procedures describe the standard case. A proportion of real events do not arrive in that shape, and the trained behaviour is to proceed sensibly and say what you decided and why. Consolidate where it genuinely improves clarity and separate where detail would be lost, but decide and move.

drills.prompt: A new unidentified object has appeared alongside a red asset. Which procedure do you enter?

accept: separation
separation first, discovery later if it stays unidentified

partial.note: Exactly right, including the sequencing.

reject.why_wrong: Unidentified is the normal condition at this point and is not what selects discovery. The parent is known and red, so this is a separation. Going straight to discovery bypasses the assessment considerations specific to a separation, and was observed happening during exercise activity.

drills.explain: They are sequential stages of one event, not alternative paths. An object separating from a red asset is a separation. If it remains unidentified after that processing, discovery follows. The trap is that unidentified feels like it should select discovery, and it does not: what selects discovery is the absence of an identified parent.

drills.prompt: Two products, two identifiers, apparently two objects. Are they?

accept: no, identical states, it is one object in two representations
no, same object, one product has put the numeric form in the name field

partial.note: Right. The check that proves it is comparing states and epochs, which are identical.

reject.why_wrong: Their orbital elements and epochs are identical. Two objects do not share a state. This is one object represented two ways across products, which was observed across more than one provider.

drills.explain: Compare states and epochs to settle it, then read which field you are actually looking at, because some products place the numeric representation in the name field while keeping the alpha-numeric form as the identifier. A common standard is still being agreed, so the trained skill is recognising the ambiguity rather than knowing which form is correct.

drills.prompt: The launch location has arrived in minutes and seconds. The procedure needs degrees. What do you do?

accept: convert deliberately and have it checked before it enters any product
convert, verify against the known site, then proceed

partial.note: Yes, and the check is the scored part. A mis-converted coordinate produces a coherent, plausible and wrong target set.

reject.why_wrong: Minutes and seconds treated as decimal degrees puts the launch site a long way from where it is, and every downstream product will be internally consistent and wrong.

reject.value: convert in my head and carry on
reject.why_wrong: This is the moment of maximum time pressure in the whole procedure, which is exactly when mental arithmetic fails silently.

drills.explain: The conversion is trivial in isolation and error-prone at tempo, which is why it is worth practising rather than assuming. Sanity-check the result against the known launch site: a mis-converted coordinate usually lands somewhere implausible, and noticing that is faster than re-checking the arithmetic.

drills.prompt: The event calls for a procedure you have never applied. What do you do?

accept: say it is unfamiliar, work from the procedure text explicitly, flag ambiguities rather than resolving them silently
state the gap and work from the text openly

partial.note: Correct, and saying out loud that you are doing so is the part that protects everyone else, because it tells the crew how much weight to put on your output.

reject.value: apply it from memory as best I can
reject.why_wrong: You have no memory of it to apply. Improvising silently converts a training gap into an assessment error that nobody can see.
Reasonable if someone genuinely knows it, but if the procedure is new to the cell then nobody does, and the gap needs naming rather than passing.

drills.explain: A procedure issued shortly before an exercise with no preparatory training meant crews were building understanding at the same moment they were applying it, and the exercise ended up testing initial understanding rather than application. When that happens to you, naming it is the professional response. It is also the observation this application most directly answers: a procedure is content here, so it can be drilled before it enters service rather than during.

drills.prompt: Compose the verbal notification for this event. Not a summary of what you would say.

accept: composed wording naming each object by identifier and role, the event, the time, and the assessment with confidence

partial.value: a description of what the call would cover
partial.note: Describing the call is not making it. The wording is the artefact, and it is scored against the same must-state list as a written report.

reject.why_wrong: A notification that can be satisfied by marking it done teaches exactly the habit to avoid. Simulating notifications by posting in a thread rather than exercising the real process was recorded as removing the opportunity to build the skill at all.

drills.explain: Every mandatory notification in this package requires produced wording rather than a completion flag, and this drill exists because of a direct observation that treating notifications as notionally complete removes the chance to build or assess the skill. Compose it as you would say it, with each object named by identifier and role.

drills.prompt: Grade this report against the quality ladder and say what is missing.

accept: level one, no pattern of life comparison and no impact statement
bare observation, missing the so-what

partial.note: Correct level. Name the two gaps: whether this is normal for the object, and what it means for anyone.

reject.value: it is fine, the observation is precise
reject.why_wrong: Precision about the observation is not the issue. Everything stated is true and a recipient still cannot tell whether it matters. Only 38 per cent of the corpus contains any impact statement, which makes this the single most common gap in real reporting.

drills.explain: Three questions in order: what happened, is this normal for this object, what does it mean. This report answers only the first. A no-impact statement is a complete answer to the third and is far better than silence, because silence and no impact read identically to the recipient and only one of them is an assessment.

drills.prompt: Find every quantity in this report that a reader could misread.

accept: the drift rate has no direction, and the elements do not say whether they are changes or values

partial.value: the elements could be changes or absolutes
partial.note: The most serious one. The drift rate also lacks an east or west direction, which is the most commonly omitted qualifier in real reporting.

reject.why_wrong: It does. Units on delta-v are well handled across real reporting, at over 99 per cent. Direction on drift rates is the actual gap, at under 30 per cent.
Present is not the same as readable. Fewer than a third of drift rates in real reporting carry a direction, and a rate without a direction is half a number.

drills.explain: Direction on every rate, and the word Change on every delta. Across real reporting, delta-v almost always carries units, but **fewer than a third of quoted drift rates carry an east or west direction**. A drift rate without a direction tells the reader the object is moving and not which way, which is the half that matters. The standard specifics block spells out Change on every line for the same reason.

drills.prompt: This report hedges three times and states no confidence. Fix it.

accept: attach a confidence level to the assessment
replace the hedges with what is known and what is not, or size them

partial.note: Wrong direction. The hedging is probably appropriate; what is missing is the size of the doubt.

reject.why_wrong: Unsized hedging is not caution, it is ambiguity. Of the corpus narratives that hedge, fewer than one in ten also state a confidence level, leaving roughly two thousand reports that signal doubt without letting the recipient judge whether to act.

drills.explain: Hedging is correct and unsized hedging is not. The fix is to add the size rather than remove the hedge. The possible-versus-verified register is a coarse two-state signal and is not a substitute: the corpus uses a possible register in three quarters of reports and states a confidence level in under eight per cent.

drills.prompt: Four minutes into a time-critical event. Which report level do you produce?

accept: level one, a holding alert, immediately
one sentence now, assessment later

reject.why_wrong: Right content, wrong moment. A calibrated report issued forty minutes late is worse than a one-sentence alert at four minutes, and the corpus shows a median of two reports per event with a maximum of thirty-six. Later reports are the norm, not a failure of the first.

drills.explain: Decide the level the moment warrants before writing. Early in a time-critical event that is deliberately a level one, and issuing it fast is the scored behaviour. The ladder is not a quality ranking to always maximise; it is a match between content and moment.

drills.prompt: Raise this level two report to level three. What do you add?

accept: a pattern of life comparison with the reasoning, and the resulting geometry and who is affected

partial.note: Half of it. The other half is consequence: what the resulting geometry means and for whom.

reject.value: more element sets from other providers
reject.why_wrong: That adds length, not level. Two states showing agreement is enough; say that sources agree rather than appending every one. Breakup reports in the corpus average around five thousand words at only moderate completeness, which is the clearest evidence that length is not quality.

drills.explain: Level three adds the two questions that turn a record into intelligence: is this normal for this object, and what does it mean. Give the pattern of life claim its reasoning so a reader can disagree with it. Note that not-station-keeping and not-in-pattern-of-life are different claims, and holding both at once is precise rather than contradictory.

drills.prompt: Three element sets are appended. What is wrong with how they are presented?

accept: no provider named and no time current for any of them
missing provenance, so staleness cannot be judged

partial.note: And no time the state was current, which is the one that prevents a staleness check.

reject.why_wrong: Three is defensible if they show agreement, though saying sources agree is usually tighter. The defect here is provenance: 23 per cent of corpus states carry no provider and 40 per cent no time current.

drills.explain: The element set epoch tells you when the solution is valid. The time it was current and who produced it are separate facts, and without them a downstream reader can neither assess staleness nor reconcile against another provider. Annotate confidence inline where a state is weak, rather than leaving it in prose.

drills.prompt: How many reportable facts are in this provider post?

reject.why_wrong: The post both verifies a manoeuvre previously reported as possible and flags a new possible one. The verification closes an open loop with the recipient and is a reportable fact in its own right. Reporting only the new item leaves them holding a possible that is no longer possible.

drills.explain: This exact situation produced a report that had to be corrected before release: the analyst wrote up the new possible manoeuvre and did not realise the same post verified the earlier one. Read the whole post and the thread above it before writing. A verification is not housekeeping; it changes what the recipient believes.

drills.prompt: You have just opened the thread. What do you request?

accept: only the pass schedule
just what is missing, the rest is already posted

partial.value: check what is already there first
partial.note: Right instinct and the scored answer is the specific gap: everything but the pass schedule is already present.

reject.value: the standard product set for this event type
reject.why_wrong: Three of the four are already posted, in one recorded case directly above the request. The procedural step is request the products you need, not paste the request. Asking a stretched provider to re-send what they have already sent costs them time and costs you minutes.

drills.explain: This was recorded as happening almost invariably, including one thread left for twenty minutes waiting on products that had already been posted elsewhere. Look above the thread as well as in it, establish what is genuinely absent, and ask only for that.

params.unresolved: whether the plane deltas are closing

drills.prompt: You need something from the provider. Write the request.

accept: a specific named product, what it will resolve, directed to the provider by name

partial.note: Named the product, which is most of it. Add what it will resolve and tag the provider, who is tracking many concurrent threads.

reject.why_wrong: A generic request signals activity without producing anything, and cannot be tracked by a provider working across twenty threads. It was assessed as analysts showing proactivity without knowing what to ask for, leaving the provider or supervisor to work it out.

drills.explain: Name the product, say what it resolves, tag the recipient, and ask verbally if speed matters. If you cannot name the product, the real problem is that you have not yet worked out what question you are trying to answer, and that is worth thirty seconds before you type.

drills.prompt: The debris came from a friendly satellite. Do you still attach the debris states?

accept: yes, debris is tracked for what it will hit, not for what it came from
yes, origin does not change the hazard

partial.note: Correct. The reason is the scored part, because it is the reason that lets you handle the next unfamiliar case.

reject.value: no, it belongs to a friendly object
reject.why_wrong: This reasoning was used in a real event and delayed the report by about an hour. Debris is tracked because of what it will hit. Its origin has no bearing on the hazard it poses to everything else in that regime.

drills.explain: An earlier exercise recommendation put it plainly: the gap is the why. A procedure learned as a sequence gives you nothing to reason from when a case falls outside the sequence. Every step in this package carries its purpose for exactly this reason. If you cannot state why a step exists, you are not in a position to judge that it does not apply.

drills.prompt: You have picked up this event. Which stage is it at, and what is your first action?

accept: it has already launched, work the current stage
post launch, tracking and target verification, not pre-launch

partial.note: Correct read. Name the action that follows, because the pre-launch product you might otherwise prepare has been overtaken.

reject.why_wrong: The launch has already occurred. Preparing a pre-launch product delayed a first report on a time-critical event in a real case. Check the most recent post and the clock before reaching for the procedure's first step.

drills.explain: When you join an event already running, establish where it sits before choosing an action. The procedure's first step is the first step of the event, not the first step of your involvement.

drills.prompt: The provider reports one large manoeuvre. Does the element signature support that?

accept: no, no single burn direction explains this combination, ask whether there were two
no, challenge the summary

partial.note: Correct. Say why: name the element combination that no single burn direction produces.

reject.why_wrong: Under high manoeuvre rates solvers struggle once burns sum together, and two manoeuvres solved as one produces an inaccurate proximity picture and incorrect categorisation. The provider described this limitation themselves.

drills.explain: A single in-track burn moves period and eccentricity. A single radial burn leaves period alone. A combination no single direction explains suggests a summed pair. Cross-check against the relative motion plot, where a summed solution often fails to match the observed geometry. Challenging a provider summary is a competency, not an impertinence, and the provider would rather you did.

drills.prompt: Which trace is the post-manoeuvre state?

accept: read the legend, the convention is not fixed between deliveries

partial.note: That is the whole answer.

reject.value: the colour it was last time
reject.why_wrong: The colour assignment for pre and post manoeuvre plots has been observed changing between deliveries, and standardising it is an open recommendation. Reading from memory of the last plot inverts the interpretation.

drills.explain: Three conventions have now been recorded as varying between providers or deliveries: relative motion plot colours, waterfall time direction, and identifier representation. They are drilled as one habit rather than three facts. Read the legend, the axis labels and the field definitions before reading the data, including on a product you have read a hundred times. Confidence is what makes this one dangerous.

drills.prompt: Your connection is intermittent but nothing has needed you yet. Do you say anything?

accept: yes, declare it now at the start of shift
yes, it will block something at the moment I am needed

reject.value: no, raise it if it becomes a problem
reject.why_wrong: It becomes a problem at the moment you are required to act, which is the worst possible moment to discover it. This was observed more than once, with issues raised only once analysts were required to act on their threads.

drills.explain: A problem that is not yet blocking is still reportable, because the cost of declaring it early is a sentence and the cost of declaring it late is a thread nobody was working. The same applies to anything that would affect your ability to act: access, tooling, or needing to leave.

drills.prompt: A clear photometric change on a friendly high rate revisit object. What do you do?

accept: do not report unless higher headquarters specifically directs, and mark the thread accordingly
open the thread with the do-not-report marker in the title, no report

partial.note: Correct decision. Carrying it in the thread title is what stops a later analyst publishing it.

reject.why_wrong: Clarity of the change is not what decides this. Photometry on a friendly high rate revisit object is not reported unless higher headquarters specifically directs it, and the check comes before the analysis.

drills.explain: Two suppression rules apply before any analysis: objects on the exclusion list, for which no event is opened at all and no mission information or element sets appear in any report, and friendly high rate revisit photometry, which is not reported unbidden. Put the decision in the thread title so it travels with the event rather than being rediscovered.

drills.prompt: A new peak has appeared. Is this a real change?

accept: not yet, only one sensor sees it, request the sensor view
cannot say, single sensor abnormality is one of the three scepticism triggers

partial.note: Right caution. Name the trigger: abnormality from a single sensor, and the check that settles it.

reject.value: yes, a new peak is one of the five change signatures
reject.why_wrong: It is, and that is only half the assessment. The five signatures tell you what a real change looks like; the three scepticism checks tell you whether this one is real. Single-sensor abnormality is the first of them.

drills.explain: Five signatures to look for: a sharp change with hard angles, a new feature, a complete change to an existing feature, a stable curve becoming a diffuse trend, and a total trend change in a single period. Three reasons to be sceptical: a single sensor, a source that saw the object before and does not see this, and a hemisphere difference. Both halves are needed, and running the scepticism checks is faster than being wrong.

drills.prompt: A close approach falls inside the change window. Is it the cause?

accept: not on this geometry, the lighting was unfavourable
no, timing alone is not a mechanism

partial.note: Check lighting before saying possibly. Favourable lighting is what converts a co-timed approach into a plausible mechanism.

reject.value: yes, it is co-timed and close
reject.why_wrong: Timing and distance make it a candidate, not a cause. Favourable lighting means sunlight positively illuminating one satellite without blinding the other. Without it, the approach does not explain a signature change.

drills.explain: State time, distance and lighting together, because the recipient needs all three to judge the claim. Where lighting was unfavourable, the close approach is worth reporting as present and worth explicitly excluding as the cause, which is a stronger assessment than leaving it implied.

drills.prompt: This object has a numeric identifier above the five-digit range and an Alpha-5 designator. Which goes in the report?

accept: both, together, so they can be cross-referenced

partial.note: Both are required. Carrying only one is what produced the inconsistency observed across provider products.

reject.why_wrong: Neither alone is correct where both exist. Providing both together is what lets a reader reconcile the identifier against the element set.

drills.explain: Alpha-5 replaces the leading digit of a five-digit catalogue number with an alphanumeric character, leaving the remaining four digits unchanged, which is also how you spot that two apparent objects are one. Reports carry both forms. This resolves an ambiguity that was observed across products from more than one provider, though provider products will continue to vary until the convention propagates.

drills.prompt: You reported this change. It turns out to have been hemispheric bias. What now?

accept: cancel the event and issue a report saying it did not meet event criteria
publish a cancellation, do not just close it

partial.note: Closure ends an event that happened. This one did not, and the recipients of the original are still holding it.

reject.why_wrong: Everyone who received the original still believes it. A cancellation is a positive act with its own report, and issuing one costs far less credibility than leaving a wrong assessment standing.

drills.explain: Cancellation is a defined outcome, not a failure state. Where an event proves not to have met criteria, say so plainly in a report and record the reasoning in the thread. Analysts avoid this because it feels like admitting error; it is the opposite, and a cell that cancels cleanly is trusted more, not less.

drills.prompt: Which pairing on this table most warrants attention?

accept: the one where sustained close approach possible is true
read the sustained approach column, not the association band

partial.note: The bands and the sustained approach column are independent. A nearby pairing with sustained approach false can matter less than a more distant pairing where it is true.

reject.value: the one with the smallest deltas
reject.why_wrong: Small deltas describe the present. Sustained close approach possible describes what the geometry permits, which is what an object would need in order to do anything.

drills.explain: Sustained close approach possible is the most directly actionable field on any product in this package: it answers whether an object could linger near the primary rather than merely pass it, and lingering is what enables collection, inspection and everything beyond. Read it before the deltas, then use the association band and the countdown to right ascension zero to understand how the situation is developing.

drills.prompt: Two objects are shown as CLOSE. What do you check before believing it?

accept: the band definitions in the header
what the thresholds for close were set to on this run

partial.note: Useful, and the header is what tells you whether those deltas earned the label. The bands are configurable.

reject.why_wrong: Association status is a banding of four continuous quantities against thresholds set in the tool. The same pair can be close under one configuration and none under another, so the label means nothing without the definition.

drills.explain: Four thresholds per band, tightening from nearby through close to same. Read the header before a single status value. Note also that the primary compared against itself appears as same with zero deltas; that row is a sanity anchor rather than a duplicate, and its absence would be the thing to worry about.

drills.prompt: You can see a change. What is the fastest way to test whether it is real?

accept: switch display mode to sensor hemisphere and then to sensor
change the display mode, the checks are on this screen

partial.note: Right check, and you do not need to request it. It is a display mode on the plot already open.

reject.value: assess it as real and report
reject.why_wrong: Two of the three scepticism checks are a selector away and take seconds. On this seed the hemisphere mode would have shown the change disappearing once north and south are separated.

drills.explain: The photometry procedure lists three reasons to be sceptical, and two of them are display modes on the light curve itself: colour by hemisphere, and colour by sensor. Switching mode is the check. This makes failing to run them considerably harder to justify, and it is why this drill has a short time target.

drills.prompt: Nine sensors are covering the period. Is corroboration good?

accept: no, they are all in one hemisphere
no, count independent geography rather than bars

partial.note: Correct. Name why: nine sensors in one hemisphere is one failure mode wearing nine names.

reject.why_wrong: Density is not diversity. Sensor rows carry site country identifiers, and where they all sit in one hemisphere the schedule cannot support a hemispheric bias check on any photometric assessment made from that period.

drills.explain: This is the product that quietly answers two of the three photometric scepticism checks, because it is where the geographic and hemispheric spread of collection is visible. Locate the present on the timeline first, then read how many genuinely independent sites cover your period of interest.

drills.prompt: Large RAAN separation, but the countdown column shows a finite value. What is happening?

accept: the planes are converging naturally, it is a countdown to alignment
slow plane match in progress using altitude rather than fuel

partial.note: Yes. The significance is that this route costs almost nothing but time, which makes it easy to run and easy to miss.

reject.why_wrong: Current separation describes now. A finite countdown with a closing rate describes where this is going, and it is the patient, fuel-cheap route to a plane match.

drills.explain: Read the countdown alongside the rate. Zero in the countdown can mean aligned now or no convergence at all, and only the rate separates those two readings. This is the mechanism an adversary uses when they have time and would rather not spend fuel, and nothing dramatic happens on any single day.

drills.prompt: The threatened operator is ready to manoeuvre now, hours before intercept. What do you advise?

accept: prepare now, move after the terminal adjustment
do not move yet, an early mover can be retargeted by in-flight updates

partial.note: Right call. Say why, and say what they should be doing instead: reallocating users, selecting an evasion plan, uploading commands, warming thrusters.

reject.value: move immediately, they have the warning
reject.why_wrong: The ascending vehicle may receive in-flight trajectory updates, and precision targeting needs a substantial window of tracking data resolved before the terminal burn. A target that moves inside that window is simply retargeted, and the manoeuvre is wasted.

drills.explain: This inverts the instinct every operator brings from conjunction avoidance, where earlier is always better. Debris does not retarget; a guided vehicle receiving updates does. Warning time exists so the asset can prepare rather than act: reallocate users, select or generate an evasion plan, upload emergency commands, warm the thruster catalyst beds. Movement has effect once the intercept path is committed, because divert capability on the final path is limited.

drills.prompt: The lighting at projected intercept sits outside the band an electro-optical seeker would need. Does that matter?

accept: yes, it makes a combat engagement less plausible and belongs in the assessment
yes, seeker lighting is a targeting constraint on the adversary

partial.note: Say why. Lighting constrains what the adversary can hit, not only what you can see.

reject.value: no, lighting only affects our collection
reject.why_wrong: It affects both. Assuming an electro-optical seeker, the target must be illuminated while the launch site is not, which means a full daytime launch is a poor fit for an engagement. It costs nothing to check and it sharpens the assessment before any tracking exists.

drills.explain: The sharpest predictive constraint in the direct ascent procedure and the one most often overlooked, because operators think of lighting as a collection issue. Treat it as a weak indicator on its own and a sharpening one alongside other cues, and state it in the assessment either way.

drills.prompt: An object of interest manoeuvred ahead of a close approach. Assess it.

accept: avoidance within pattern of life, the manoeuvre increased the resulting distance
distance keeping, consistent with prior cycles

partial.note: Correct. The pattern of life comparison across prior cycles is what makes it a finding rather than an observation.

reject.value: manoeuvre of intent, it is closing on our asset
reject.why_wrong: Check the effect. The resulting distance increased. This object has done the same thing across several prior cycles, keeping approaches above a consistent floor.

drills.explain: Some objects of interest manoeuvre specifically to keep their distance, consistently and for years. An operator who treats every manoeuvre by such an object as significant will over-report constantly, and the genuinely anomalous one will then not stand out. Check the effect on the resulting distance and compare against prior cycles before assessing intent.

drills.prompt: Two objects launched together have just performed similar inclination changes. What is the assessment?

accept: coordinated activity across the launch group, a third member already did this
a campaign rather than individual manoeuvres

partial.note: Correct effect. The finding is that this is coordinated across the group and that an earlier member set the precedent.

reject.why_wrong: Common launch, similar magnitudes, and the same set of objects being matched. Coincidence does not produce all three, and a group member did the same thing days earlier.

drills.explain: The first object to move is the indicator and the rest are confirmation, which only becomes obvious in retrospect unless you are reading across objects rather than down a thread. When something notable happens to an object, check what else launched with it and what those objects have been doing.

drills.prompt: A very slight inclination change on an object with two years of history. Reportable?

accept: yes, it is the first time this object has been observed changing inclination
yes, novelty rather than magnitude is the finding

partial.note: Say why. Small and unprecedented are different claims, and the second is what makes this reportable.

reject.why_wrong: Magnitude is the wrong test here. An object with two years of history that has never changed inclination doing so at all is the finding, and stating that it is the first observed instance is what makes the report land.

drills.explain: This directly counters weighting significance by magnitude. A slight change on an object that has never done it is more informative than a large routine station-keep. Check the history before dismissing on size, and where it is unprecedented say so explicitly in the report.

drills.prompt: The signature you reported yesterday has returned to normal. Do you report the return?

accept: yes, it closes the loop and the transience is evidence about the original
yes, a return to pattern of life is a reportable change

partial.note: Correct. The second reason is the more interesting one: a transient departure and a permanent one mean different things.

reject.why_wrong: Everyone who received the original is still holding it. The return closes their loop, and it is also evidence: knowing the departure lasted about a day changes what it could have been.

drills.explain: Under-reported consistently, and it costs almost nothing. Report the return explicitly, and use its duration in reassessing the original change rather than treating the two as separate events.

drills.prompt: The determination table reports one manoeuvre. The relative motion plot shows the geometry changing twice. Which is right?

accept: the plot, two burns were summed into one solve
the relative motion, challenge the solve

partial.note: Correct observation. Say which you believe and why: geometry changes are observations, a solve is an interpretation.

reject.value: the determination table, it has the numbers
reject.why_wrong: Numbers are not evidence of being right. The relative motion shows two discrete geometry changes, which no single burn produces. Under high manoeuvre rates solvers sum burns that occur close together.

drills.explain: A solve is an interpretation of observations; the relative motion geometry is closer to the observations themselves. When they disagree, prefer the one further upstream and challenge the other. This is the reconciliation habit that no single-product drill can build, and it maps directly to a recorded real failure where an analyst could not connect a solve to a picture that did not match it.

drills.prompt: A residual departure. Use the pass schedule to decide whether to believe it.

accept: the pass schedule shows a collection gap across the departure, so the fit decayed
no, the gap explains it

partial.note: Right, and the pass schedule is where you check it. The gap is visible there before it is visible in the residuals.

reject.value: a manoeuvre, the departure is clear
reject.why_wrong: The departure is clear and the pass schedule shows why. A starved fit produces exactly this picture, and the second product settles in seconds what the first cannot settle at all.

drills.explain: Two products, one answer, and neither gets there alone. The residual plot shows something changed; the pass schedule shows whether there was enough data to know. Reaching for the second product is the composite skill, and it is what separates an analyst from a reader of plots.

drills.prompt: A photometric change. Can it be corroborated from the collection you have?

accept: no, the pass schedule shows all coverage from one hemisphere
no, there is no independent geography to corroborate with

partial.note: Correct check, and the pass schedule tells you the answer before you switch: there is only one hemisphere in the data.

reject.why_wrong: Several sensors in one hemisphere is one failure mode wearing several names. Density is not diversity, and the pass schedule is where you see that.

drills.explain: The photometry procedure's hemisphere check needs the pass schedule to be answerable. This is the cross-product link the package previously never made, and it means an operator assessing a light curve should have the pass schedule open too.

drills.prompt: The neighbourhood shows a close approach. The relative motion shows the objects passing quickly with wide cross-track separation. Reconcile.

accept: a transient pass, not a proximity relationship
they close in longitude but not in plane, so neither can linger

partial.note: They do not, actually. A small miss distance and a fast wide-separation pass are consistent, and together they say transient rather than significant.

reject.why_wrong: Distance alone is not the assessment. The relative motion shows the objects cannot stay near each other, which is what turns a number into a judgement.

drills.explain: Two products that appear to conflict and actually complement. The neighbourhood gives you the number; the relative motion gives you whether the number means anything. Lingering is what enables everything, and a fast pass enables nothing.

drills.prompt: Build the assessment. Three products are available.

accept: the step change coincides with a lit close approach, which is the likely cause
photometry gives the change, neighbourhood the candidate, relative motion the lighting

partial.note: That is one product's worth. The other two supply the cause and whether the geometry supports it.

reject.why_wrong: Unknown is honest when nothing explains it. Here a lit close approach falls inside the window, which is a mechanism rather than a coincidence, and the products to establish it are all present.

drills.explain: Three products, one assessment. The light curve says what changed and when; the neighbourhood offers a candidate; the relative motion says whether lighting made the candidate plausible. This is what producing an assessment actually looks like, and it is the shape the package previously never trained.

drills.prompt: The plane match is complete. What can this object now do that it could not yesterday?

accept: close on the matched object cheaply and quickly, because the expensive part is already paid for
it now has a low-cost route to proximity that it did not have

partial.note: That is what happened. The question is what it enables, and the answer is that closure is now cheap.

reject.value: nothing, it has only changed inclination
reject.why_wrong: Plane matching is the expensive part of reaching another object. Having paid it, everything afterwards is cheap, which is exactly why the plane match rather than the approach is the warning.

drills.explain: An event matters because of the options it creates. This is the weakest question in both the package and four years of released reports, and it is the one that makes a report actionable rather than informative. Ask what the recipient would now do differently, and if the answer is nothing, ask whether you have finished the assessment.

drills.prompt: The object has parked. Who is affected, and how?

accept: nobody, and say so explicitly in the report
no objects of interest at this longitude, stated as a finding

partial.note: Correct, and the scored part is that it goes in the report. Silence and no impact read identically to a recipient.

reject.value: leave it out since there is no impact
reject.why_wrong: A no-impact statement is a complete answer and a strong one. Omitting it leaves the recipient unable to tell whether you checked.

drills.explain: An explicit no-impact statement scores fully here, because it demonstrates the question was asked. The failure is not concluding no impact, it is not saying so. Note that consequence content is reasonably well handled in real reporting; **pattern of life assessment, at around a third of reports, is the weaker half of this pair** and is what most often turns an observation into an assessment.

drills.prompt: An object catalogued as a spent upper stage has manoeuvred. What does that tell you?

accept: it is not a spent upper stage, either the catalogue is wrong or it is not what it appears
the classification is wrong, and that is the finding

partial.note: Yes, and the significance is that this class cannot. Use the cannot list to eliminate.

reject.why_wrong: A spent upper stage has no propulsion available to it. An object that manoeuvres is not one, whatever the catalogue says, and that mismatch is itself reportable.

drills.explain: The cannot list does more analytical work than the can list, because it eliminates hypotheses outright. Reason from behaviour to class, never from catalogue label to expectation.
