drills.prompt: A staged, deliberate closure to contact. Servicing or attack?

accept: not distinguishable by geometry, report capability and observation and state that intent is not observable

partial.note: Correct, and the report still has plenty to say: what was observed, what capability it demonstrates, and that intent is not observable from it.

reject.value: servicing, that is the stated mission
reject.why_wrong: A stated mission is publicly available information, hedged and kept separate from the observation. It is not evidence about this approach.
Same geometry either way. Whose the target is does not change what the observation supports.

drills.explain: The clearest case in the domain where capability and intent must be reported separately, because no geometric discriminator exists. The strong report says exactly what was seen, what it demonstrates the object can do, and that intent cannot be read from it. That is a more useful product than a confident guess in either direction.

drills.prompt: A manoeuvre on an object of standing interest, matching its established cadence exactly. Escalate?

accept: no, report as routine within pattern of life
no escalation, state the pattern of life finding

reject.value: yes, it is an object of interest
reject.why_wrong: Standing interest is not a reason to escalate every manoeuvre. Eight prior cycles at the same cadence and magnitude make this housekeeping, and escalating it spends attention that the anomalous one will need.

drills.explain: Over-reporting erodes the alerting channel the cell exists to serve. A pattern of life assessment that concludes routine is a real finding and should be reported as one, without escalation.

drills.prompt: A close approach with no manoeuvre to sustain it, one pass only. Open a proximity event?

accept: no, this is a close approach rather than proximity operations
no, nothing is being sustained

partial.note: Right. Name the discriminator: proximity operations require the geometry to be maintained, and nothing here maintains it.

reject.why_wrong: Proximity operations means actively staying within a controlled vicinity. A single unforced pass with no manoeuvre is a close approach, and the two carry different reporting obligations.

drills.explain: The discrimination between a close approach and proximity operations is definitional and consequential. One pass with no sustaining manoeuvre is not an RPO, and opening one commits the crew to a procedure the event does not warrant.

drills.prompt: A brightness variation below the notification threshold and consistent with this object's normal range. Report?

accept: no, below criteria and within pattern of life
no report, record the assessment

partial.note: Correct. Record that you assessed it, because a decision not to report is a decision worth having on the record.

reject.value: yes, any change should be reported
reject.why_wrong: The threshold and the pattern of life comparison exist precisely to prevent that. Reporting normal variation trains recipients to ignore the channel.

drills.explain: Knowing when not to report is a competency in its own right and the package previously trained it about twenty-seven times less than acting. Record the decision and the reasoning; the assessment happened even though the report did not.

drills.prompt: An object has been held at elevated tasking for its full profile duration and nothing further has emerged. What now?

accept: step the rank down per the profile
reduce tasking, it is holding capacity others need

reject.value: keep it elevated to be safe
reject.why_wrong: Collection capacity is finite. Holding a rank beyond its profile duration is a decision that should be taken deliberately with a reason, not reached by omission.

drills.explain: Tasking is a schedule rather than a single decision, and ranks step down on a timetable. Extending is legitimate where there is a reason; extending by forgetting is how collection capacity quietly disappears.

drills.prompt: The launch time has slipped by twenty-two minutes. The nominal is already out. What follows?

accept: re-rotate to the new time, redistribute, and re-run the in-plane or apogee assessment

partial.note: Necessary and not sufficient. The at-risk set changes with RAAN, so the assessment is re-run too.

reject.value: nothing, twenty-two minutes is close enough
reject.why_wrong: Launch time determines RAAN. A nominal rotated to the wrong time is right in size and wrong in plane, which looks correct and sends collection to the wrong part of the sky.

drills.explain: Rotation errors were recorded as a recurring source of wasted collection, including providers working from differently rotated nominals simultaneously. Re-rotate, redistribute, and re-run.

drills.prompt: A candidate track, before separation, with nothing identified. Report or wait?

accept: report now, the procedure requires it as soon as a candidate track is obtained
publish, identification follows later

reject.value: wait until separation so the payload can be named
reject.why_wrong: The procedure states a report should be distributed as soon as a candidate track is obtained, even prior to payload separation. A named payload in a late report is worth less than an unnamed one on time.

drills.explain: The most explicit latency instruction in any procedure in the package, and it says the same thing as the direct ascent timeline and the corpus evidence: publish early, refine later.

drills.prompt: Three passes, no track. Has the launch failed?

accept: not established, reassess the nominal first
no, a nominal wrong in plane looks identical to an absent object

partial.note: Right. The action is the scored part: reassess the nominal before assessing the launch.

reject.why_wrong: Three misses says you are not looking in the right place, and the two most likely reasons are that the object is not there or that the nominal is wrong. Only one of those is about the launch.

drills.explain: Acquisition failure is not launch failure. A nominal wrong in plane is right in size and produces exactly this picture, and reassessing it is usually more productive than a fourth attempt.

drills.prompt: The object is in low orbit and bound for the belt. How do you state its orbit?

accept: state the current parking orbit and the intended destination separately
currently in a parking orbit with these characteristics, final destination the belt at this longitude

partial.note: Half the answer. A reader given only the current orbit will conclude it has arrived.

reject.value: state the destination, that is where it is going
reject.why_wrong: It is not there yet and the transfer may take weeks. Both facts are needed, stated separately, or the reader draws the wrong conclusion from either alone.

drills.explain: Two facts, stated separately: where it is and where it is going. A transfer to a higher regime can take weeks, and the event stays open across it because the destination is the reportable outcome.

drills.prompt: An object has stopped drifting. Is where it parked significant?

accept: yes, the neighbourhood shows what it parked next to and whose slot it is
the park is not the event, the location is

partial.note: That is the waterfall's answer. The neighbourhood tells you whether it matters.

reject.why_wrong: Parking is routine; parking here may not be. The waterfall cannot tell you what is at that longitude and the neighbourhood can.

drills.explain: The waterfall gives you the behaviour and the neighbourhood gives you the meaning. Neither is sufficient, and the habit of reaching for the second is the whole of tier one.

drills.prompt: A large photometric expansion, and early fragment states. What can you say about the event energy?

accept: the spread of the Gabbard arms indicates energy, but the fragment set is early and is a floor
tentative, the fragment data is too sparse to characterise energy confidently

partial.note: Established by the photometry. The energy question needs the fragment distribution, and that data is not yet mature.

reject.value: low energy, the spread is narrow
reject.why_wrong: Early fragment counts are a floor rather than a total, so a narrow spread this early may just mean the cloud has not been correlated yet.

drills.explain: Two products, and the second is not yet ready to answer. Recognising that a product cannot yet support the question is as much a synthesis skill as reading it.

drills.prompt: Sustained close approach is possible. How confident can you be in the current picture?

accept: limited, the pass schedule shows a two-day coverage gap
the geometry allows it but the states are old across the gap

partial.note: That is the coplanar product. The pass schedule tells you how current the inputs to it are.

reject.value: high confidence, the column says true
reject.why_wrong: A computed judgement inherits the currency of the states behind it. The coverage gap means the geometry may have changed since anything was observed.

drills.explain: A derived judgement is only as current as its inputs. Pairing an analytic product with the collection picture behind it is the fastest way to calibrate confidence, and it is almost never done.

drills.prompt: Optical merged, photometry merged, element sets converged, and no radio frequency data. Docked?

accept: consistent with a merged condition but not established, the discriminating phenomenology is missing
cannot confirm, all three indicators share the same failure mode at close separation

partial.note: Say why it is only probably: all three of your indicators degrade the same way at close separation, so three agreeing is not three independent confirmations.

reject.why_wrong: They agree because they share a limitation. Optical merging, photometric merging and element set convergence all follow from the objects being unresolvable, which is exactly what happens whether or not they touched.

drills.explain: The sharpest lesson in synthesis: agreement between products that share a failure mode is not corroboration. Three optical-derived indicators saying the same thing is one indicator. Ask what would have to be independent for this to be confirmation, and here that is radio frequency, which is absent.

drills.prompt: Out-of-plane departure, an inclination change, and the coplanar table. What is this object doing?

accept: a deliberate plane change accelerating closure with another object
it has spent fuel to bring the planes together faster

partial.note: That is the first two products. The coplanar table tells you what the burn was for, which is the assessment.

reject.why_wrong: Accurate and incomplete. The coplanar table shows the closure accelerating, which converts a manoeuvre into an intent finding.

drills.explain: Three products in sequence, each narrowing the last. The residual says out of plane, the determination table says how much, and the coplanar table says what it bought. The third is where description becomes assessment.

drills.prompt: Headcount of two on a red parent. Build the picture.

accept: a deliberate separation co-timed with a parent burn, with an unranked object inside the new reach
separation, and the neighbourhood shows something at risk that the ranked view would hide

partial.note: Established. The residuals give you the co-timed burn supporting intent, and the neighbourhood gives you who is in reach.

reject.value: headcount of two, awaiting more information
reject.why_wrong: You have three products and they answer what happened, whether it was deliberate, and who it affects. Waiting is not the gap here.

drills.explain: What happened, was it deliberate, who does it affect. Three products, three anatomy questions, one assessment. Note the unfiltered neighbourhood: the ranked view would have hidden the object that matters.

drills.prompt: Five products. What is happening, and why do you believe it?

accept: a conclusion with each part attributed to a product, one alternative eliminated, proportionate confidence, a falsifier, and the gaps

partial.note: That is the conclusion. Tier three asks for the argument: which product supports which part, what you ruled out and how, and what would change your mind.

reject.value: all five products are consistent with a plane match
reject.why_wrong: Consistency is not an argument. Name which product carries which part of the claim, and say what you eliminated.

drills.explain: The first tier that asks for an argument rather than an answer. Six components: conclusion, evidence chain, eliminated alternative, proportionate confidence, falsifier, gaps. Note that one of the five products contributes nothing here, and recognising that is part of the skill: opening everything is not the same as using everything.

drills.prompt: A real photometric change with two candidate causes. Argue for one.

accept: a conclusion naming the more likely cause, with the evidence for it, the evidence against the alternative, and what would settle it

partial.note: Legitimate, and at tier three you are asked to argue. Say which is more likely and why, then state the observation that would settle it.

reject.why_wrong: True and not an assessment. Rank them, say why, and name what would discriminate. A recipient can act on a ranked judgement and cannot act on a list.

drills.explain: Ambiguity is not an excuse to withhold judgement, it is the condition under which judgement is worth something. Rank the candidates, attribute the evidence, and name the discriminating observation. That is a report an operations centre can use.

drills.prompt: The solve and the geometry disagree. Build the argument for what actually happened.

accept: two burns summed into one solve, with the residuals and relative motion carrying the claim and the solve identified as the weak link

partial.note: Probably right. The argument needs which products carry the claim, why they outrank the solve, and what would confirm it.

reject.why_wrong: They are, and that is the starting point rather than the finding. Say which you believe, why, and how confident that leaves you.

drills.explain: Confidence is set by the weakest link in the chain, not the strongest. Here the residuals and geometry are strong and the solve is weak, so the assessment is confident about what happened and explicitly provisional about the numbers.

drills.prompt: Full board. A staged closure to contact. Produce the assessment.

accept: capability demonstrated and stated, intent explicitly not observable, evidence chain across the board, falsifier named

partial.note: The observation may support a merged condition. The assessment must separate what was observed, what capability it demonstrates, and what cannot be read from geometry.

reject.value: a servicing mission per the stated purpose
reject.why_wrong: A stated mission is publicly available information, hedged and separate. It is not evidence about this approach, and the same geometry serves refuelling and capture.

drills.explain: The full board on the hardest discrimination in the domain. A strong assessment here is confident about the observation, confident about the capability, and explicitly silent on intent, with each part attributed. Every anatomy question should be answered from evidence.

drills.prompt: Full board, four objects from one launch. What is the campaign, and what does it enable?

accept: a coordinated campaign across the group with the enablement stated, evidence attributed per object, and a falsifier

partial.note: The effect. Tier four asks what the campaign enables, which object leads, and what would show you were wrong about the coordination.

reject.why_wrong: Common launch, similar magnitudes, same objects being matched, staggered timing. Reading across objects rather than down threads is the whole point of the full board.

drills.explain: Reading across objects is what the full board makes possible and what a single thread never will. The campaign is visible only in aggregate, and the enablement question is what turns it into a warning.

drills.prompt: Full board on an ascending object with an apogee near the belt. Assess and advise.

accept: an assessment of the likely target set with the lighting reasoning stated, and advice distinguishing preparation now from movement later

partial.note: The classification. The assessment needs the target longitude reasoning, the lighting plausibility, and the timing advice, which is the part that helps the asset.

reject.value: advise the target to manoeuvre immediately
reject.why_wrong: In-flight updates retarget an early mover. The advice is to prepare now and move after the terminal adjustment, and getting that wrong costs the asset its one manoeuvre.

drills.explain: The highest-consequence full-board item. It combines target assessment, the seeker lighting constraint, and the counterintuitive timing advice. An assessment that is analytically correct and advises movement too early has failed the asset it was written for.

drills.prompt: Contested board. One provider is down, several states are stale, and two products disagree. Assess anyway.

accept: a stated conclusion with the unresolved contradiction named rather than hidden, confidence pegged to the weakest link, and a falsifier

partial.value: cannot assess, the data is degraded
partial.note: Degraded data is the normal condition. The skill is assessing anyway and being explicit about what you could not resolve.

reject.value: a confident assessment ignoring the conflict
reject.why_wrong: A contradiction you have not mentioned is one the recipient will find later, and it takes the whole assessment down with it. Name it and say why it does or does not change the conclusion.

drills.explain: The advanced capstone. Real events arrive degraded and contradictory and still need an assessment. Distinguish a contradiction that changes the conclusion from one that does not, state both, and peg confidence to the weakest link rather than the strongest.

drills.prompt: Contested board, sitting right on the reporting threshold. Assess, then defend it.

accept: a clear recommendation with reasoning, held or revised under challenge on the evidence

partial.note: Correct process. Tier five asks you to make the recommendation as well, and then to defend or revise it.

reject.why_wrong: Deferring is not assessing. Make the recommendation, own the reasoning, and change it if the challenge is good.

drills.explain: Revising correctly under challenge scores higher than defending a weak position. That is deliberate: the mechanic rewards calibration rather than stubbornness, and an analyst who cannot change their mind on good evidence is a liability regardless of how often they are right.

drills.prompt: Contested board. The object has gone quiet and the collection picture only partly explains it. Assess.

accept: exclusion explains part of the gap but not all of it, stated as a partial explanation with the residual unexplained and a falsifier

partial.note: Explains part. Tier five is about the part it does not explain, and saying so is the assessment.

reject.value: nothing to assess, it is in exclusion
reject.why_wrong: The exclusion window does not cover the whole gap. The unexplained remainder is the finding, and dismissing the whole absence on a partial explanation is how a real event gets missed.

drills.explain: A partial explanation is the most dangerous kind, because it satisfies the instinct to explain and stops the analysis. Establish how much of the gap the benign explanation actually covers, and treat the remainder as the finding.

drills.prompt: Indication at zero, last provider product at ten minutes, it is now twenty-two. When is your report due?

reject.why_wrong: The 30 minute leg from the last provider product governs here, because products arrived at ten minutes. Your deadline is forty, not sixty, and you have eighteen minutes left rather than thirty-eight.

drills.explain: Two clocks, and the earlier one governs. Fast provider delivery tightens your window rather than relaxing it, which is counterintuitive and is exactly why it is worth drilling. Recompute whenever a further product lands.

drills.prompt: GEO object, period change of 14 seconds, negligible plane change, Rank 2. Manoeuvre or station-keeping, and what do you produce?

accept: station-keeping, and at Rank 2 that warrants both a written report and a verbal call
SK, both report and verbal

partial.note: Correct classification. The rank determines what you produce, and at this rank it is both.

reject.why_wrong: In the belt, a manoeuvre requires a period change above the higher threshold or a plane change at or above the criterion. Fourteen seconds with negligible plane change sits in the station-keeping band.
Station-keeping is still reportable at higher ranks. Classification and reporting obligation are separate questions.

drills.explain: Two questions, in order. The regime and the period change decide whether it is a manoeuvre or station-keeping. The object's rank then decides whether you produce a written report, a verbal call, both, or nothing. Thresholds differ by an order of magnitude between regimes, so carrying one number across all three is a reliable way to be wrong.

drills.prompt: A small station-keeping burn in the belt on a Rank 4 object. What is owed?

accept: nothing
no report at this rank for a burn of this size

partial.note: Effectively right. The reporting matrix returns no obligation at this rank and magnitude.

reject.why_wrong: Reporting every small station-keep on a low-ranked object would swamp the channel. The matrix exists precisely to prevent that.

drills.explain: Knowing when nothing is owed is a competence. The reporting matrix runs from both a written report and a verbal call at the top, through verbal only, to nothing at all. An operator who reports everything erodes the value of the alerting channel they depend on.

drills.prompt: An object is using right ascension drift to close on a friendly high reportable satellite. Three days to closure. What now?

accept: publish and raise the rank, this has crossed the middle condition threshold
report and uprank

partial.note: Half of it. Crossing this threshold raises the tasking rank as well as triggering the report.

reject.value: monitor, it is still three days out
reject.why_wrong: The ladder exists so that tasking rises before arrival rather than after. Three days is a defined escalation point, not a comfortable margin.

drills.explain: An escalation ladder on days to closure, not on current separation. Each threshold crossed raises both the reporting obligation and the collection rate, and the crossing happens on a day when nothing visibly changes. That is exactly why it is written down as a ladder rather than left to judgement.

drills.prompt: A new Rank 2 object needs passive radio frequency collection. Both providers are at capacity. What do you do?

accept: establish which provider can track its bands at all, then identify the lowest priority object to drop and escalate the swap
check band capability first, then propose the swap to the site lead

partial.note: Right principle. Check band capability first, because only one provider may be able to track this object at all.

reject.why_wrong: Capacity is contracted in fixed slots. There is no additional capacity to request, and treating this as an administrative step rather than a trade wastes the time the swap decision needs.

drills.explain: Passive radio frequency collection is contracted in a fixed number of slots across two providers with different band coverage. Every addition is a subtraction. Establish band capability first, because it may make the decision for you, then bring the swap to the site lead as a priority judgement rather than an administrative request.

drills.prompt: A previously merged pair has manoeuvred together, off the element set of either object. Assess.

accept: capture, one object is manoeuvring the other and relocating it
capture rather than merge

partial.note: They are, and the manoeuvre changes the assessment. A merged pair moving as one under control is capture.

reject.why_wrong: Cross-tagging produces an apparent merge from a tracking limitation. It cannot produce a coordinated departure from the original element set, because no tracking artefact moves an object.

drills.explain: The taxonomy is a ladder of seriousness: close approach, series of close approaches, perch, merge, capture, intercept. Merge is proximity too close to resolve. Capture is the merged pair manoeuvring as a single body, which means one object is moving the other. Getting the word right matters because each one carries a different response.

drills.prompt: A tracked object with no catalogue entry appears in your sweep with a close approach. How do you treat it?

accept: treat as friendly, perform a stability assessment, do not raise its tasking
as a blue object with a stability assessment and no tasking increase

partial.note: Correct, and two things follow: a stability assessment is required, and its tasking is not increased.

reject.value: skip it, it has no rank
reject.why_wrong: Unranked objects are not processed, and Known Objects are the explicit exception to that rule.
A Known Object is tracked and understood. It simply lacks a catalogue entry, which is a records problem rather than an identification problem.

drills.explain: A Known Object is a tracked object familiar to analysts with no catalogue entry, and providers label them inconsistently. Treated as friendly, requires a stability assessment, and tasking is not raised on it. Skipping it because it has no rank is the error the exception exists to prevent.

drills.prompt: A drifting red object has a close approach inside criteria in 40 hours. Drift rate is steady. Raise the rank?

accept: no, it is drifting through, watch for a decrease in drift instead
no, proximity without slowing is geometry

partial.note: Correct. Name what would change it: a decreasing drift rate, which suggests the object intends to park.

reject.value: yes, it is inside the criteria
reject.why_wrong: A drifting object passes through many close approaches and almost none of them mean anything. The procedure is explicit that rank is not raised for close approaches while drifting, unless the drift is decreasing.

drills.explain: Slowing is the signal, not proximity. A drifting object will produce a close approach every few days as it crosses the belt, and raising the rank on each would consume collection capacity permanently. Watch the drift rate; a decrease near an object of interest is what warrants attention.

drills.prompt: An object with known longitude bounds is drifting and now sits three degrees from one of them. What do you do?

accept: raise to the higher rank until the turn-around completes, and post a potential activity alert
uprank and alert, watching for proximity operations at the turn

partial.note: Correct, and say why: a turn-around is coming and it is where proximity operations occur.

reject.why_wrong: Within the margin of a bound, a turn-around is predictable. The object will slow, reverse, and do so near whatever is at that longitude, which is exactly the geometry proximity operations need.

drills.explain: Objects operating within established longitude bounds turn around at the limits. The bound predicts when the object will slow and reverse, and a turn-around near something of interest is an opportunity. Anticipating it is the point of the whole procedure.

drills.prompt: A close approach of 26 km is forecast in 68 hours, on an object whose pattern is to manoeuvre away below 30 km. What do you produce?

accept: a potential activity alert forecasting a manoeuvre
an alert that the object may manoeuvre due to the upcoming approach

partial.note: Correct forecast. It is posted as a potential activity alert, which is a distinct product from an event report.

reject.why_wrong: Nothing has happened. An alert anticipates behaviour; a report records it. Publishing a report on a manoeuvre that has not occurred is a different error from failing to anticipate one.
Anticipating the behaviour is more useful than recording it afterwards, and if the expected manoeuvre does not occur, that absence becomes the finding.

drills.explain: This is the most sophisticated move in the procedure: predicting adversary behaviour from pattern of life and saying so in advance. It also sets up the more interesting case. If you forecast a manoeuvre and it does not happen, the object has departed from its own pattern, and that is a stronger finding than the manoeuvre would have been.

drills.prompt: A friendly asset has manoeuvred and now sits within collection range of a red object. What do you open?

accept: a do-not-report thread, held for 24 hours to gather observations and confirm the asset is clear

partial.note: Marked do-not-report, so nothing is published outward, and held for a day.

reject.why_wrong: The subject is our own asset and the exposure is ours. This is tracked internally, not broadcast.
Exposure is exposure whoever created it. The thread exists so the asset is watched until it is clear of the geometry it moved into.

drills.explain: A whole class of event that is easy to miss because the analysis looks outward by habit. When a friendly asset manoeuvres, ask what it has moved next to. If the answer is a red object's collection or approach range, that is tracked internally on a do-not-report thread and held until the asset is clear.

drills.prompt: A plane change of 0.12 degrees in the belt, on an object with a regular RAAN flip cadence. Manoeuvre of interest?

accept: no, assess as a RAAN flip station keep and process as station-keeping
not if it is associated with a RAAN flip station keep

partial.note: Correct. The qualifier is specific: a plane change meeting the criterion is still processed as station-keeping when it is a RAAN flip.

reject.value: yes, it exceeds the plane change criterion
reject.why_wrong: The criterion carries an explicit qualifier. Where the change is associated with a RAAN flip station-keeping manoeuvre, it is treated as a station keep for processing.

drills.explain: Meeting a numeric criterion is not sufficient on its own. A plane change large enough to qualify can still be routine if it is a RAAN flip station keep, and the discriminator is the object's own cadence. Check the history before classifying on the number.

drills.prompt: Launch site latitude is 45.6 degrees. What inclination band do you filter targets across?

reject.why_wrong: The lower bound sits five degrees below launch latitude, because a dogleg profile can reduce achievable inclination below the naive minimum.
An unfiltered band produces a target list nobody can act on. The filter is what makes the warning specific.

drills.explain: Start five degrees below launch site latitude, because a dogleg can reduce achievable inclination below what the latitude alone suggests. The upper bound is 180 minus the start inclination, covering retrograde. Get this wrong and the target list is wrong, and everything downstream inherits the error while looking entirely coherent.

drills.prompt: A 12 second period change at navigation altitudes. Roughly what delta-v is that?

reject.why_wrong: About 33 seconds of period change per metre per second at that altitude, so 12 seconds is roughly a third of a metre per second.

drills.explain: Carry one number per regime: roughly 84 seconds of period change per metre per second in the belt, 33 at navigation altitudes, 2.3 in low orbit. The useful consequence is that the three published notification thresholds all convert to between a quarter and one metre per second, so they are one idea expressed three ways rather than three numbers to memorise.

drills.prompt: A mid-ranked object appears in the threat geometry. Is it a concern?

accept: cannot tell from rank, read the state of behaviour separately
rank is attention warranted, not hostility

partial.note: Exactly. At the middle ranks the population is close to an even split between friendly and otherwise.

reject.value: yes, it is ranked so it matters
reject.why_wrong: Rank expresses routine attention, not hostility. The middle ranks carry legacy friendly systems, hosted payloads and commercial partner systems, and roughly half that population is friendly.

drills.explain: Rank and state of behaviour are independent readings. The highest standing rank is entirely red, the middle ranks are close to an even split, and the lowest is dominated by retired and proliferated objects. An operator who treats rank as a threat scale will misread the middle of the list, which is where most of the population sits.

drills.prompt: An object was elevated for an event that closed 30 hours ago. It is still elevated. What now?

accept: return it to its standing rank, or extend deliberately with a reason

partial.note: Right. Extending is legitimate with a stated reason; extending by omission is not.

reject.value: leave it, more collection is better
reject.why_wrong: Collection is finite and the high ranks are deliberately a small set. An elevation held past its event consumes cadence that another object needs, and the top ranks are temporary tasking by definition.

drills.explain: The top two ranks are temporary tasking elevations rather than standing categories. Every elevation has an end, and the governing procedure states the duration. Extending is a decision; extending by forgetting is how collection capacity quietly disappears.

drills.prompt: You have identified a friendly object inside the crossing band. Separation has not occurred. What goes in the report?

accept: the object, without its state
name it but withhold the state until after separation

partial.note: Correct, and the omission is the scored part: the state is deliberately withheld at this phase.

reject.why_wrong: The state is withheld before separation. Naming the object warns its operator; publishing the state offers precision to anyone reading who should not have it, while the engagement is still being aimed.

reject.value: nothing until the picture is firmer
reject.why_wrong: The operator needs the warning. It is the state, not the identification, that is held back.

drills.explain: A deliberate and subtle rule. Before separation the at-risk object is named and its state is not. After separation and an initial orbit determination, the state is released, because by then the engagement is committed and the warning value to the operator outweighs what the state gives away. Disclosure changes with phase, and the reasoning is worth understanding rather than memorising.

drills.prompt: Compose the verbal notification to operations centres. Four potential targets are identified.

accept: give the affected longitude window, not the individual target names

partial.value: report the event and the crossing
partial.note: Right shape. The specific rule is that the window is given and the names are not.

reject.value: read out the four target identifiers
reject.why_wrong: The verbal notification carries the longitude window. The names go in the written report, which travels more controllably.

drills.explain: Two channels, two contents, on purpose. The verbal call gets the warning out fast across a wide audience and carries the affected longitude range. The written report carries the target list. An operator who gives the same content on both has not made an error of analysis, but has made one of disclosure.

drills.prompt: Maximum altitude is 35,820 km. Which longitude do you assess against?

accept: the apogee longitude, it is inside the tolerance band

partial.note: Correct. It sits about 34 km above the belt, inside the tolerance, so apogee remains the centre longitude.

reject.why_wrong: That applies where apogee is materially above the belt. Within about fifty kilometres the apogee point is still the centre longitude, and choosing the penetration point here would shift the target list.

drills.explain: Belt altitude is not a hard line. There is a tolerance of roughly fifty kilometres, and an apogee inside it still uses the apogee longitude. Getting this wrong shifts the whole target list, which is why it is the first analytical decision in the procedure.

drills.prompt: Sensors have searched the posted trajectory and found nothing. What next?

accept: extend the search several minutes along track and a few degrees across track

partial.note: Correct. The procedure gives the shape: several minutes along track, a few degrees across.

reject.why_wrong: A state vector converted into a trajectory carries error in both timing and geometry. Absence on the exact line is expected rather than informative, and the search is widened before any conclusion is drawn.

drills.explain: The trajectory is an estimate built from a single state vector. Searching only the exact line and reporting nothing found is the same error as concluding a launch failed because three passes missed: it treats a prediction as if it were an observation.

drills.prompt: An event has been briefed. What is missing?

accept: the next steps and the current checklist step
the two forward-looking points

partial.note: One of two. The current checklist step is the other, and it tells you where in the procedure the event sits.

reject.why_wrong: Thoroughness about the past is not clarity about the next action. Six points are required and the two most often dropped are the two that carry forward.

drills.explain: Six points: why it was opened, who tasked what to which rank, which timers affect your shift, what reporting is done, next steps, and the current checklist step. The last two are the ones that save you re-deriving position and intent from a thread you have not read, while an event is running.

drills.prompt: You have raised an object's rank for an upcoming close approach. What must go in the record alongside it?

accept: the thread reference, the object, the reason, and an expiry date

partial.note: And the expiry, which is the part that makes the step-down happen.

reject.why_wrong: An elevation without an expiry becomes permanent by omission. Nothing will prompt the step-down and the collection capacity stays consumed.

drills.explain: Reason and expiry travel with the object. The top ranks are temporary tasking by definition, so every elevation has an end, and the expiry in the record is the mechanism that makes it happen rather than relying on someone remembering.

drills.prompt: Twenty-five minutes to changeover. Six events worked, one record entry. What is the problem?

accept: the handover is already compromised, the record does not reflect the shift

partial.note: And the consequence: what gets briefed will be what is remembered, not what happened.

reject.value: nothing, there is time to update it now
reject.why_wrong: Reconstructing six events at changeover produces a brief built from memory. A shift briefed as quiet when it was not has been recorded happening, and the incoming crew inherited a false picture.

drills.explain: Handover quality is decided hours before handover. The record is maintained through the shift or the brief becomes a recollection, and the failure is invisible to the crew giving it because they remember the shift they had.

drills.prompt: A routine daily check has not been done today. Is that a problem?

accept: check the allocation first, it may belong to another cell on this day

partial.note: Exactly. Allocation varies by cell and weekday, and assuming coverage is the failure mode.

reject.value: no, another cell will have done it
reject.why_wrong: Assumed coverage is how a routine check lapses without anyone noticing. Read the allocation rather than recalling it.
Duplicating another cell's task wastes capacity and can conflict. Establish ownership first.

drills.explain: Daily tasks are divided across cells and weekdays rather than repeated everywhere. From inside one cell, a task owned by another and a task missed look identical, and only the allocation distinguishes them.

drills.prompt: Which of the changes in the delta column were produced by the manoeuvre, and how do you know?

accept: period
semi-major axis
apogee
perigee
the in-plane elements
inclination
not the RAAN
RAAN is natural drift

partial.note: Right instinct, wrong reason. Say which elements and why the large ones moved on their own.

reject.value: the RAAN change, it is the largest
reject.why_wrong: Size is not evidence. Over a fit interval of a day and a half the node regresses several degrees on its own for an orbit of this inclination and altitude. The large number is the one that needed no burn.
The delta column is change across the fit interval, and natural secular drift happens inside that interval whether or not anything manoeuvred.

drills.explain: The delta column is not the manoeuvre. It is the difference between two states separated by the fit interval, and over that interval the node regresses and the perigee rotates under the Earth's oblateness alone. For this orbit the right ascension change is what natural regression would produce across the interval on its own. The manoeuvre is in the small in-plane numbers: the period change of a fraction of a second and the semi-major axis change of under a tenth of a kilometre. Read the fit interval first, every time, then ask what would have moved anyway.

drills.prompt: This object was raised into the ranks that attract dedicated collection this morning and has no rows from the constrained sensor type. State the rule that has been triggered and what has to happen next.

accept: capacity is full, an object must be de-tasked
swap out a lower priority object
the mission area lead decides which object to drop
nominate an object to remove
raised into the tasking band so dedicated collection is required

partial.note: Reasonable first move but it does not resolve anything. The provider cannot add capacity it does not have under contract.

reject.value: wait for the geometry to improve
reject.why_wrong: This is not a geometric gap. Nothing changes as the passes come round, because no capacity was freed.

reject.value: nothing, the rank change is enough
reject.why_wrong: The rank change is the trigger for the tasking, not the tasking itself. Recorded and unresourced is the failure mode this cue exists to catch.

drills.explain: Dedicated collection of this type is bought in fixed object counts. Crossing into the ranks that require it does not create capacity, it creates a trade. Somebody loses custody so this object can gain it, and that decision belongs to the mission area lead rather than to the provider. The competence being trained is noticing that an elevation has a cost and naming who pays it, rather than assuming the request resolves itself.

drills.prompt: This draft is ready to publish. Is it correct as it stands, and why?

accept: no, strike the target element set
no, the target is friendly so its set is withheld
no, remove the appended target state
not correct, target element set must come out

partial.value: no, something is wrong with the states
partial.note: Correct call, incomplete reason. Name which set and the rule that removes it.

reject.value: yes, all three sets are held and current
reject.why_wrong: Holding the data is not the test. Against a friendly target the target's element set is withheld regardless of how good it is.

reject.value: no, none of the element sets should be published
reject.why_wrong: Overcorrection. The actors' sets are the substance of the report. It is the target's set that comes out.

drills.explain: Disclosure is decided by what the target is, not by what is held. Actor against a red target, the target set goes in. Actor against a friendly target, it does not. For a protected object or a well-tracked uncorrelated track nothing positional is published at all, and the report refers only to its presence in the area. The failure mode is appending everything the product had, at the last step, when the drafting attention has already moved on.

_new_response_formats.cross_product_reconciliation: Requires two or more products and asks the operator to resolve where they disagree. Added after the red team found zero of 81 drills referenced more than one product.
_new_response_formats.anatomy_question: Asks a single event anatomy question about a presented event, weighted towards what it enables and who is affected, which are the weakest questions in both the package and the corpus.
_new_response_formats.no_action_correct: Drills where the correct answer is no report, no escalation or an explicit statement of no impact. Added to correct a twenty-seven to one imbalance towards acting.
_new_response_formats.reasoned_argument: Tier three and above. The operator states a conclusion, an evidence chain naming which product supports which part, at least one eliminated alternative with its evidence, a proportionate confidence, a falsifier, and the gaps. Scored on argument structure rather than on a single right answer.

_generator_contract.note: CANONICAL. Ten product renderers and two composition modes. Earlier drill authoring used ad-hoc generator names; those are preserved as _legacy_generator in params for traceability and MUST NOT be implemented.
_generator_contract.build_instruction: Implement exactly the twelve generators below. Each product renderer is a hand-written class registered against its product_id. The two composition modes orchestrate renderers; they are not renderers themselves.

waterfall.note: Dense observation scatter, tens of thousands of points, realistic collection gaps. Newest at bottom. Not clean traces.

residual.note: Tight y-scale, a few hundredths. Series labelled time and beta association. Supports a manoeuvre marker with period and inclination deltas.

dc_table.note: Initial, Final, Delta columns in fixed order. Also renders draft reports and element-set comparisons. CORRECTED 31 Aug 2026: an earlier note read Initial, Delta, Final, which is not the observed screen order.

light_curve.note: Magnitude against solar equatorial phase angle. Magnitude axis INVERTED. Display modes: interval, sensor hemisphere, sensor.

tric.note: Six panels, INDEPENDENT per-panel scales. Time gradient along track. State change markers distinct from manoeuvres.

neighbourhood.note: Full column set including delta-v, score, days to longitude crossing. Threshold block in header. Filter toggles visible in real state.

coco.note: ASTAT bands, coplanar angle, RA dot, days to RA zero, sustained close approach possible boolean. Band definitions in header.

pass_schedule.note: Timeline, one row per sensor with site identifiers. Now marker plus node, apogee and perigee crossings. Group by source or phenomenology.

ephemeris.note: State vector series with reference frame stated. Also renders ascent profiles and launch nominals.

gabbard.note: Apogee and perigee altitude against period. Parent orbit marked.

composite.note: Presents two or more renderers together for cross-product reconciliation. params.products lists product IDs, or 'all' for the full board. params.tier sets the synthesis tier.

probe.note: Presents a scenario state and asks a single anatomy question or a no-action judgement. Uses whichever renderer the params name; adds no rendering of its own.

_generator_contract.registry_requirement: Each renderer registers against its product_id. The content validator asserts every product referenced by a drill or scenario has a registered renderer, so content pointing at an unbuilt product fails at load rather than at runtime.
_generator_contract.contract_tests: Tests read the generator_contract block in product-layouts.json and assert each renderer honours it. When a layout is corrected, the test fails and names the renderer.
